objections.objection: The body text gives HR 0.510 as the three-year recurrence result, but 0.510 is the five-year figure; the three-year figure is HR 0.501.
objections.quote: By the three-year readout at ASCO 2024, since published in full, the interval no longer crossed it: HR 0.510, 95% CI 0.288–0.906
objections.why: The draft holds the JCO Oncology Advances three-year paper and cites it as a source. That paper reports HR 0.501 at three years, not 0.510. HR 0.510 is the five-year point estimate, reported in the five-year JCO paper and the ASCO 2026 data. The CI (0.288–0.906) is correct for the three-year readout, so the interval has been correctly assigned to the wrong point estimate. A reader checking the three-year paper against this sentence will find a discrepancy in the headline number.
objections.fix: Change 0.510 to 0.501 in this sentence. The five-year figure (0.510) is already correctly stated elsewhere in the piece.

objections.objection: The subheading 'The distinction the coverage collapsed' accuses the coverage of collapsing a distinction that the body immediately below it says the coverage did not collapse.
objections.why: The very next paragraph states: 'Every outlet whose article we hold attributed those figures correctly to KEYNOTE-942.' A subheading is a claim, and this one directly contradicts the finding reported beneath it. A reader who reads only the subheading takes away the opposite of what the body establishes. This is a contradiction within the piece.
objections.fix: Replace the subheading with something that reflects what the body actually argues — e.g. 'Why correct attribution is not enough' or 'What correct attribution still leaves open.'

objections.objection: The sentence 'That is what the headlines did' accuses unnamed headlines of substituting Phase 2b figures for Phase 3 figures without attribution, but the draft has established that every outlet it holds attributed correctly.
objections.quote: That is what the headlines did.
objections.why: The draft names five outlets and says all of them attributed the figures correctly to KEYNOTE-942. It then says 'that is what the headlines did' — meaning the substitution without attribution. The draft holds no example of a headline that performed this substitution without attribution. The accusation is directed at unnamed third parties and is unsupported by any instance the draft can point to. This is the same class of error the draft's own correction log flags: an accusation against coverage that the outlet-by-outlet check does not sustain.
objections.fix: Replace with a sentence that describes the structural problem without accusing unnamed outlets of doing something the draft cannot evidence — e.g. 'The structure of the coverage creates that effect even when attribution is correct.'

objections.objection: The lede frames the coverage as having failed ('what was actually released, what was not') in a way the body substantially retracts, creating a misleading first impression.
objections.quote: Several outlets called it a landmark. This is what was actually released, what was not, and what the numbers underneath it will and will not support.
objections.why: The juxtaposition of 'Several outlets called it a landmark' with 'This is what was actually released' implies the landmark characterisation was unwarranted or that the coverage misled. The body then says most specialist outlets attributed figures correctly and several explicitly noted no Phase 3 numbers had been released. Calling a first positive Phase 3 mRNA cancer therapy result a landmark is not obviously wrong. The lede sets up a critique the body does not deliver.
objections.fix: Separate the two sentences or reframe: acknowledge the result is genuinely significant before pivoting to what the numbers do and do not show, so the lede matches the body's more nuanced conclusion.

objections.objection: The comparison table note says the Phase 3 is 'blinded against the assessment bias the earlier one carried,' but the draft's own next paragraph says the investigator-assessed endpoint means the bias is only substantially reduced, not eliminated.
objections.quote: It is the more trustworthy trial by a wide margin — seven times larger, and blinded against the assessment bias the earlier one carried.
objections.why: The phrase 'blinded against the assessment bias' implies the bias is fully addressed. The paragraph immediately following says the Phase 3 defines its primary endpoint as recurrence 'as assessed by the investigator' and that this 'leaves clinical judgement in the endpoint.' The draft's own correction log records that an earlier version said 'exactly' this bias and was softened — but 'blinded against' still overstates relative to what the next paragraph says. The two sentences are in tension.
objections.fix: Change to 'substantially blinded against the assessment bias the earlier one carried' to match the qualification the very next paragraph provides.

objections.objection: The draft says the April 2023 press release is 'the source of the one-sided p = 0.0266' and implies this value may appear nowhere else, but the ASCO 2023 abstract (LBA9503) also reports the same one-sided p = 0.0266.
objections.quote: We have not opened the conference abstract of the same analysis, so this page does not say the one-sided value appears nowhere but here.
objections.why: The draft is careful to hedge ('this page does not say the one-sided value appears nowhere but here'), which is honest. But the source note still singles out the April 2023 press release as the source in a way that implies the value is unusual or company-only. The ASCO 2023 abstract (LBA9503), which is publicly available, also reports the one-sided p = 0.0266 alongside the same HR and CI. The hedge is sufficient but the framing could mislead a reader into thinking the one-sided value was suppressed in academic venues.
objections.fix: Add a parenthetical noting that the ASCO 2023 abstract also reports the one-sided value, or remove the implication that the press release is the sole source.

inferences.quote: the interval around it runs from a hazard ratio of 0.165 — a rate of death about 84% lower than the comparison group's — to 1.345, about 35% higher. Both ends are rate comparisons, not numbers of lives.
inferences.problem: The draft correctly defines both ends as rate comparisons, but the lower bound description ('a rate of death about 84% lower') is arithmetically imprecise: HR 0.165 means the hazard is 83.5% lower, which rounds to 84% — that is fine — but the phrasing 'a rate of death about 84% lower than the comparison group's' could be read as an absolute rate reduction rather than a relative hazard ratio. More importantly, the draft has already warned readers that a hazard ratio is not a headcount and is not an absolute risk reduction; describing the lower bound in percentage-reduction language without repeating that caveat in the same sentence risks the very misreading the explainer was written to prevent. This is a minor internal consistency issue, not a factual error.
inferences.correct_reading: HR 0.165 means the instantaneous hazard of death in the treated group was estimated at about one-sixth of the control group's hazard at any given moment — not that 84% of deaths were prevented. The upper bound of 1.345 means the hazard could be about a third higher in the treated group.
inferences.fix: the interval around it runs from a hazard ratio of 0.165 — meaning the treated group's rate of death was estimated at roughly one-sixth of the control group's at any given moment — to 1.345, meaning it could be about a third higher. Both ends are instantaneous rate comparisons, not counts of lives saved or lost.

inferences.quote: At one end the treated group's rate of death would be about a sixth of the control group's; at the other it would be about a third higher.
inferences.problem: This is a second instance of the same sentence-level hazard-ratio-as-rate-comparison phrasing appearing without the caveat that this is a relative hazard, not an absolute risk reduction. The draft's own explainer box states 'The value is a rate, not a headcount' and that an HR 'does not mean 49% of patients were saved.' Describing the lower bound as 'about a sixth' is correct as a ratio statement but, appearing in the body text four paragraphs after the explainer, a reader who skips the box will read 'a sixth of the control group's rate of death' as an absolute claim. The draft contradicts its own instruction to the reader by not repeating the relative-rate caveat at the point of use.
inferences.correct_reading: HR 0.165 means the instantaneous hazard of death was estimated at roughly one-sixth of the control group's hazard — a relative rate comparison, not an absolute risk reduction. HR 1.345 means the hazard could be about a third higher. Neither bound converts directly into a count of lives.
inferences.fix: At one end the treated group's instantaneous hazard of death would be about a sixth of the control group's — a relative rate, not a count of lives; at the other, the hazard could be about a third higher.

inferences.quote: no randomised trial against placebo has reported a statistically significant overall survival benefit as a prespecified endpoint in its own population
inferences.problem: The draft qualifies this claim carefully ('as a prespecified endpoint in its own population'), but the claim as written is about adjuvant PD-1 inhibitors in melanoma specifically. The EORTC1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial (adjuvant pembrolizumab vs placebo in stage III melanoma) has OS as a key secondary endpoint and has reported seven-year follow-up data; the draft does not establish whether OS has or has not been formally tested as a prespecified endpoint in that trial. If KEYNOTE-054 has a prespecified OS analysis that has not yet been formally reported as significant, the sentence is accurate; if it has been reported and is non-significant, the sentence is still accurate; but the draft asserts this without citing a source for the OS endpoint status of KEYNOTE-054, leaving the claim unverified. This is a THIRD_PARTY claim about what a trial has or has not reported, offered without evidence.
inferences.correct_reading: The EORTC1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial has OS as a prespecified secondary endpoint and has reported seven-year RFS and DMFS data with OS still maturing; no statistically significant OS benefit has been reported from that trial as of the available literature. The sentence is likely accurate but requires a citation to the OS endpoint status of KEYNOTE-054 to be defensible.
inferences.fix: no randomised trial against placebo has reported a statistically significant overall survival benefit as a prespecified endpoint in its own population [cite KEYNOTE-054 seven-year update confirming OS still maturing]

inferences.quote: The confidence interval is the range of true effects reasonably consistent with what the researchers saw.
inferences.problem: This is a common and defensible informal gloss, but it is technically imprecise in a piece that elsewhere insists on precision: a 95% CI does not contain the 'true effect' with 95% probability in a frequentist framework. It means that if the procedure were repeated many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true value. The draft's own p-value section is careful to distinguish what a p-value does and does not mean; the CI definition is held to a lower standard in the same piece.
inferences.correct_reading: A 95% confidence interval is constructed by a procedure that, if repeated across many trials, would contain the true effect 95% of the time. It is not a probability statement about this particular interval containing the true value.
inferences.fix: The confidence interval is the range of values that the trial's procedure would capture the true effect within, 95% of the time if repeated — a range consistent with what was observed, not a probability that the truth lies inside it.

inferences.quote: A one-sided test asks only 'is it better?' A two-sided test asks 'is it different, in either direction?' For a symmetric test the two-sided p-value is about double the one-sided one, so the same data gives 0.0266 one way and 0.053 the other — identical evidence, measured against a different question.
inferences.problem: The relationship 'two-sided p ≈ 2 × one-sided p' holds only when the one-sided test is in the direction of the observed effect. The draft states this as a general rule without that qualification. If the observed effect were in the opposite direction, the two-sided p would be approximately 2 × (1 − one-sided p), not 2 × one-sided p. In this specific case the direction is correct and the arithmetic holds, but the rule as stated is incomplete and could mislead a reader applying it elsewhere.
inferences.correct_reading: When the observed effect is in the direction being tested, the two-sided p-value is approximately double the one-sided p-value. Here, 2 × 0.0266 ≈ 0.053, which matches the Lancet figure. The relationship only holds in the direction of the observed effect.
inferences.fix: For a symmetric test, when the observed effect is in the direction being tested, the two-sided p-value is about double the one-sided one, so the same data gives 0.0266 one way and 0.053 the other — identical evidence, measured against a different question.

inferences.quote: widening it at both ends — down into IIB and IIC, and into IIIA, none of which the earlier trial included
inferences.problem: The draft states INTerpath-001 widened the population 'into IIIA, none of which the earlier trial included.' KEYNOTE-942 enrolled stage IIIB (with a relapse condition), IIIC, IIID, and IV — so IIIA was indeed excluded from KEYNOTE-942. INTerpath-001 enrolls stage IIB, IIC, III (all substages including IIIA), and IV. The factual claim that IIIA was not in KEYNOTE-942 is supported by the trial's eligibility criteria. However, the draft's comparison table states KEYNOTE-942 enrolled 'Stage IIIB–IV' without noting the relapse condition on IIIB, which means the table understates the restriction on IIIB entry in KEYNOTE-942. This is a minor omission in the table, not in the sentence under review, but the sentence itself is accurate.
inferences.correct_reading: KEYNOTE-942 enrolled stage IIIB (only if relapsed within 3 months of initial surgery), IIIC, IIID, and IV — so IIIA was excluded. INTerpath-001 enrolls all stage III substages including IIIA. The sentence is accurate. The comparison table's 'Stage IIIB–IV' label for KEYNOTE-942 omits the relapse condition on IIIB entry and slightly overstates the breadth of that trial's stage IIIB enrollment.
inferences.fix: In the comparison table, change 'Stage IIIB–IV resected' for KEYNOTE-942 to 'Stage IIIB (relapsed ≤3 months post-surgery), IIIC, IIID, IV resected' to reflect the actual eligibility restriction.

inferences.quote: the interval stopped including 1.0 rather than crossing a threshold anyone tested
inferences.problem: This sentence correctly characterises the three-year analysis as descriptive. However, the draft uses this phrasing in two places — once in the 'What time did to the top two bars' section and once in the 'What is established' section — and in the first location it immediately follows the statement 'the interval no longer crossed it: HR 0.510, 95% CI 0.288–0.906.' A reader of that paragraph will understand the distinction. But the second use, in the 'What is established' section ('its interval stopped including the no-effect line by year three and stayed clear — often a sign an effect is real, though the three-year analysis was descriptive rather than a formal test'), is sound. No error here; recording as checked.
inferences.correct_reading: Both uses of this phrasing are accurate and consistent with the source document's own language ('not intended for formal hypothesis testing'). No correction needed.

inferences.quote: An independent review committee would move that judgement to blinded central assessors rather than remove it
inferences.problem: This sentence is a direct repair of the recorded error DESIGN_CRITICISM_IMPORTED, which previously read 'an independent review committee would remove the judgement altogether.' The repaired sentence is accurate: an IRC relocates judgment to blinded central assessors, it does not remove it. This is correct and consistent with the recorded fix. No error.
inferences.correct_reading: The sentence is accurate. Recording as checked — the recorded error has been correctly repaired.

inferences.quote: the five-year analyses were descriptive : they were not designed to test a hypothesis. No p-value was released for this survival analysis at all, which is what a descriptive analysis means: the figures are reported, and nothing is being tested against a threshold registered in advance.
inferences.problem: The draft states 'No p-value was released for this survival analysis at all.' This is presented as a fact about what was released. The draft's own source list cites the JCO five-year paper as the source for the OS analysis. The draft does not establish whether the JCO paper itself reports or withholds a p-value for the OS analysis — it only asserts none was released. If the paper reports a nominal p-value alongside the exploratory HR (as is common even in descriptive analyses), the sentence is wrong. The draft should either cite the paper's exact language or qualify 'no p-value was released in the company announcement' rather than as a general statement.
inferences.correct_reading: The company announcement released no p-value for the OS analysis. Whether the peer-reviewed JCO paper reports a nominal p-value for the exploratory OS analysis is not established by the draft. The sentence should be scoped to the announcement, or the paper's exact treatment of the OS p-value should be confirmed.
inferences.fix: No p-value was released for this survival analysis in the company announcement, which is consistent with a descriptive analysis: the figures are reported, and nothing is being tested against a threshold registered in advance.

inferences.quote: Reported as survival rates, the same analysis reads 92.2% alive at five years versus 71.3% — 95% CI 84.2–96.3 and 35.4–89.6 . Look at that second interval: on seven deaths in fifty patients it runs from a third of that arm alive to nine in ten
inferences.problem: The draft says the lower bound of 35.4% means 'a third of that arm alive.' 35.4% is closer to one-third (33.3%) than to any other simple fraction, so the gloss is defensible. However, the draft also says the upper bound of 89.6% means 'nine in ten.' 89.6% is closer to nine in ten (90%) than to any other simple fraction, so that gloss is also defensible. No error in the arithmetic. However, the draft uses these two survival-rate bounds to illustrate the width of the OS interval, and then says 'which is another way of saying the same thing the hazard ratio says.' This is approximately true — both the HR interval and the survival-rate interval reflect the same underlying uncertainty — but they are not mathematically equivalent ways of saying the same thing: the HR interval is a ratio of instantaneous hazards integrated over the follow-up period, while the survival-rate CI is a point estimate at a single time. The draft's 'another way of saying the same thing' overstates the equivalence.
inferences.correct_reading: The survival-rate confidence interval and the hazard ratio confidence interval both reflect the same underlying data sparseness (14 deaths), but they are not equivalent representations: the HR interval summarises the hazard ratio across the whole follow-up, while the survival-rate CI is a point estimate at five years. Both illustrate the same uncertainty but from different angles.
inferences.fix: which is another way of illustrating the same underlying uncertainty the hazard ratio interval captures — both reflect fourteen deaths, seven in each arm

inferences.quote: All three are meaningful and none is a substitute for another. Adjuvant melanoma trials have a history of recurrence benefits that took years to translate into survival benefits, and sometimes never did.
inferences.problem: The sentence 'All three are meaningful and none is a substitute for another' correctly resists endpoint demotion. The immediately following sentence — 'Adjuvant melanoma trials have a history of recurrence benefits that took years to translate into survival benefits, and sometimes never did' — is accurate as a general historical observation. However, placed immediately after the statement that all three endpoints are meaningful, it functions rhetorically to re-subordinate RFS and DMFS to OS, partially undoing the preceding sentence's work. A reader will quote the second sentence alone. This is a calibration issue, not a factual error, but it is the same structural problem the draft identifies in the coverage it criticises: a correct qualification placed nearby does not repair a sentence a reader will quote on its own.
inferences.correct_reading: The historical observation about translation lag is accurate and worth including. It should be framed as a reason why OS follow-up matters, not as a reason to discount RFS and DMFS, which the preceding sentence has correctly described as meaningful in their own right.
inferences.fix: All three are meaningful and none is a substitute for another. Adjuvant melanoma trials have a history of recurrence benefits that took years to translate into survival benefits — which is why OS follow-up matters, and why the Phase 3 continues to measure it.

inferences.quote: the three-year paper says the trial was designed with approximately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.5 against a one-sided alpha of 0.10
inferences.problem: The draft attributes the 80% power and one-sided alpha of 0.10 to the three-year paper. The ASCO 2024 deck is also cited as stating the same threshold. The draft does not establish whether these design parameters apply to the Phase 2b KEYNOTE-942 or to the Phase 3 INTerpath-001. In context, the surrounding paragraph is discussing the KEYNOTE-942 p-value of 0.0266, so the design parameters cited must be KEYNOTE-942's. This is correct — KEYNOTE-942 was designed with a one-sided alpha of 0.10. No error, but the sentence should make explicit that these are KEYNOTE-942's design parameters, not INTerpath-001's, since the paragraph also discusses the Phase 3.
inferences.correct_reading: The one-sided alpha of 0.10 and 80% power to detect HR 0.5 are KEYNOTE-942's design parameters, not INTerpath-001's. The sentence is accurate but could be misread as applying to the Phase 3.
inferences.fix: the three-year KEYNOTE-942 paper says that trial was designed with approximately 80% power to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.5 against a one-sided alpha of 0.10

inferences.quote: The confidence interval is the tell: 0.309–1.017 crosses 1.0, which is exactly what a two-sided 95% interval keys on — and the same data, read against the one-sided 90% interval the trial actually registered, would not cross it.
inferences.problem: The draft asserts that the same data, read against a one-sided 90% interval, would not cross 1.0. A one-sided 90% CI lower bound for HR 0.561 with the observed data would need to be calculated; the draft presents this as a fact without showing the arithmetic or citing a source. The three-year paper reports an 80% CI of 0.351–0.743 for the recurrence HR, which does not cross 1.0, but that is a different readout and a different HR. For the 2023 first readout (HR 0.561, two-sided 95% CI 0.309–1.017), the one-sided 90% CI lower bound is not given in any cited source. The claim that it 'would not cross' 1.0 is an inference the draft presents as established fact.
inferences.correct_reading: For a one-sided test at alpha 0.10, the relevant threshold is the one-sided 90% CI lower bound (or equivalently, whether the one-sided p-value is below 0.10). The draft reports the one-sided p = 0.0266, which is well below 0.10, so the trial did clear its own threshold — that much is established. Whether the one-sided 90% CI lower bound specifically does not cross 1.0 is a separate arithmetic claim that requires either the calculation or a citation. The p-value alone is sufficient to make the point; the CI claim is unnecessary and unverified.
inferences.fix: The confidence interval is the tell: 0.309–1.017 crosses 1.0, which is exactly what a two-sided 95% interval keys on — and the one-sided p-value of 0.0266 was well inside the trial's own prespecified one-sided alpha of 0.10, so the trial cleared its own threshold by a wide margin.

inferences.quote: Most of the side effects attributed to the vaccine were mild to moderate — fatigue 59.6%, injection-site pain 59.6%, chills 51.0%.
inferences.problem: The draft correctly scopes these figures to 'side effects attributed to the vaccine specifically' (per the update log). However, the sentence structure — 'Most of the side effects attributed to the vaccine were mild to moderate' followed immediately by three high-percentage figures — implies that 59.6% of patients experienced fatigue, 59.6% experienced injection-site pain, and 51.0% experienced chills, and that these were mild to moderate. The draft does not state the grade breakdown for these specific events. If any of these three events occurred at grade 3+ in a meaningful proportion of patients, the 'mild to moderate' characterisation is incomplete. The draft elsewhere reports that grade 3+ treatment-related events overall were 25% vs 18%, but does not link that figure to these specific vaccine-attributed events.
inferences.correct_reading: The three percentages describe any-grade incidence of vaccine-attributed events. The 'mild to moderate' characterisation is the company's description of the vaccine-attributed adverse event profile overall, but the grade breakdown for these three specific events is not shown. The sentence should either show the grade breakdown or qualify that these are any-grade incidence figures.
inferences.fix: Most of the side effects attributed to the vaccine were reported as mild to moderate — fatigue 59.6%, injection-site pain 59.6%, chills 51.0% (any grade; grade breakdown for these specific events not reported in the release).

inferences.quote: It is a difference worth knowing about, not a flaw.
inferences.problem: The draft correctly notes that investigator-assessed recurrence in a double-blind trial is substantially protected against directional bias, and that regulators have approved adjuvant melanoma therapies on this basis. The sentence 'It is a difference worth knowing about, not a flaw' is a conclusion the draft reaches after that reasoning. This is a defensible editorial judgment, not a factual claim, and the reasoning that precedes it supports it. No error.
inferences.correct_reading: The conclusion is supported by the preceding reasoning and is consistent with regulatory precedent. No correction needed.

inferences.quote: Data support scores 1 — the rubric's anchor for 1 is 'no data cited.' That is not quite right here: a directional result was cited. What was not released is any magnitude, so the 1 reflects the absence of an effect size rather than the absence of a result.
inferences.problem: The draft acknowledges that scoring data support as 1 against an anchor of 'no data cited' is imprecise, because a directional result (endpoints met) was cited. It then explains the 1 as reflecting absence of magnitude. This is an honest self-correction, but the draft still assigns 1 and publishes it. A score of 1 anchored to 'no data cited' will be read by any user of the rubric as meaning no data were cited — which the draft itself says is wrong. The explanation in the body text does not repair the score, because the score is what will be quoted and shared.
inferences.correct_reading: If the rubric's anchor for 1 is 'no data cited' and the draft acknowledges that a directional result was cited, the score should either be adjusted upward (e.g., to 2, reflecting 'directional result only, no magnitude') or the rubric's anchor for this score should be explicitly redefined in the published piece. Publishing a score the piece itself says is wrong, with the correction buried in the body, is the same structural error the draft identifies in the coverage it criticises.
inferences.fix: Either adjust data support to 2 with a note that 2 reflects 'directional result cited, no effect size released,' or add a parenthetical to the score display: 'Data support 1* (*rubric anchor is no data cited; a directional result was cited — see note below)' and move the explanation to the score display itself.

Also noted the double-blind design eliminates open-label assessment bias as an explanation for the directional result, while correctly flagging that magnitude cannot be assessed.
best_coverage.still_omitted: Does not explain the width of the OS confidence interval (0.165–1.345) or the n=14 death count underlying it, does not discuss the one-sided vs two-sided p-value framing, and does not give the absolute RFS or OS landmark rates that would let a reader feel the size of the Phase 2b effect.

contradictions.quote: MLQ News: The companies have not disclosed hazard ratios, confidence intervals, p-values, median follow-up or event counts for the Phase 3 trial.
contradictions.counterexample: MLQ News actually states: 'The companies have not disclosed the Phase 3 hazard ratios, p-values, median follow-up or detailed adverse-event rates.' The words 'confidence intervals' and 'event counts' do not appear in the MLQ text found; the draft's quoted version adds two items MLQ did not enumerate.
contradictions.fix: Quote MLQ only for what it actually said: that hazard ratios, p-values, median follow-up, and detailed adverse-event rates were not disclosed. The confidence-interval and event-count items in the quoted sentence belong to the draft's own analysis, not to MLQ, and should be attributed accordingly.

contradictions.quote: One detail has had little attention. Merck's own description of the Phase 3 defines its primary endpoint as recurrence 'as assessed by the investigator' rather than by central adjudication.
contradictions.counterexample: The ASCO Post explicitly states: 'The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival, defined as the time from randomization to any disease recurrence... as assessed by the investigator, or death due to any cause.' Cancer Therapy Advisor states the same language verbatim. Both pieces published this detail at the time of the announcement.
contradictions.fix: Reframe as: 'The investigator-assessed endpoint definition appeared in the ASCO Post and Cancer Therapy Advisor, though neither piece discussed what it implies about assessment bias in the context of the double-blind design.' The claim of 'little attention' is overstated; the detail was printed, just not analysed.

contradictions.quote: Every outlet whose article we hold attributed those figures correctly to KEYNOTE-942 — The ASCO Post, Dermatology Times, Practical Dermatology, KOL Pulse and MLQ News
contradictions.counterexample: OncoDaily, Biotech Blueprint, AJMC, CancerNetwork, BioPharm International, EMJ Reviews, and Pharmacy Times also attributed the figures correctly to KEYNOTE-942 (or omitted them entirely). The list of five outlets understates the breadth of correct attribution and could imply the others did not get it right.
contradictions.fix: Expand the list or use a formulation such as 'every specialist outlet we reviewed' rather than naming only five, to avoid implying the unnamed outlets failed on attribution.

contradictions.quote: The third figure has not come back. We also removed a 'five-year topline of 20 January 2026' reporting a one-sided nominal p = 0.0075. That document is still in nothing we hold and in no source list on this page, and nothing found since has changed that.
contradictions.counterexample: The January 20, 2026 Moderna/Merck press release is publicly available (Moderna IR PDF, s2.q4cdn.com) and reports 'one-sided nominal p=0.0075' for the five-year KEYNOTE-942 RFS analysis. CancerNetwork also cites this p-value from the five-year data. The document exists and is findable; the draft's correction notice implies it may not.
contradictions.fix: The correction note should be updated: the January 20, 2026 release exists and is publicly available. The p=0.0075 figure is real and sourced. The draft should either add this document to its source list or explain why it is choosing not to rely on it, rather than leaving a reader to infer the document may be fictitious.

coverage.what_this_piece_can_add: No outlet found — including the most careful specialist treatments — explains the OS confidence interval (0.165–1.345) in terms of what its two ends mean in plain language, or connects the n=14 death count to the interval width in a way a non-specialist reader can use. The draft's walk-through of that interval, and its explanation of why 'an encouraging trend' is the only honest label for a result that spans an 84% reduction to a 35% increase, is genuinely absent from all coverage found and is the layer this piece adds that even the best specialist reporting does not.
